title: Shopping, colors and prices
objectives: I can read the words of this unit aloud and explain why each accent, digraph and nasal vowel is written the way it is.
I can ask how much something costs and understand prices from 100 to 1.000.000 in reais.
I can use este, esse and aquele, and isto, isso and aquilo, to point at things with the right agreement.
I can describe clothes and colors with the right agreement, including when the noun is left out.
I can ask for a size, say what I want to try on, and ask or bargain about payment.

vocabulary.note: Said kah-mee-ZAY-tuh: a single s between two vowels is [z], so the s is not an s sound. Feminine, as the final -a predicts. The ending -eta marks a smaller version of camisa, shirt.

Portuguese uses the singular for one pair, a calça, and the plural as calças means the same thing; English only has the plural. Spelling: cal-ça, the l closes the first syllable so it is [w] (KOW-suh), and the cedilla makes c an [s] before a.
Said SAI-uh: ai is a diphthong, one beat, so sai-a has two syllables, not three.

From English 'tennis'. One tênis is one pair; to name a single shoe you say um pé de tênis, 'a foot of sneaker'. The accent: TÊ-nis is stressed on the first syllable, but the ending -is defaults to the last, so an accent is required, and it is a circumflex because the stressed e is closed. Singular and plural are identical: o tênis, os tênis.
Said kah-ZAH-koo: s between vowels is [z]. Both c letters stand before a or o, so both are [k].
Spelling: bol-sa. The l closes the first syllable, so it is [w]; the s after a consonant is [s].
The letter j is always [ʒ], the s of 'measure': LAW-zhuh. The example has às, the crase from the accents lesson: the preposition a fused with the article as, "at the" before a plural time.
Spelling: ta-ma-nho. The pair nh is one sound [ɲ], like 'ny' in canyon, and is never split. Clothes sizes P, M, G and GG are said with letter names: pê, eme, gê, gê-gê. Shoes use o número.

The ordinary word for number; in a shoe shop it is the shoe size, as in Eu uso número quarenta e dois. The accent: NÚ-me-ro is stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so it is always marked; u has one quality, so the mark is the acute.

example.pt: Eu uso número quarenta e dois.
example.literal: I use number forty and two.

vocabulary.note: From provar, to try (on); the ending -dor names the one or the place that does the action. Stressed on the last syllable (pro-va-DOR), which is the default for -r, so no accent.

example.en: The fitting room is over there.

vocabulary.note: Four forms: branco, branca, brancos, brancas. Spelling: an before a consonant is a nasal vowel, so the n is not a consonant sound (BRAHN-koo, nasal); br has a tap r.
Four forms: preto, preta, pretos, pretas. The stressed e is closed, like the ay of 'say' held steady.

example.en: I want a pair of black sneakers.

vocabulary.note: One form for masculine and feminine. Plural azuis: a final l becomes is. Said ah-ZOOW: z between vowels is [z] and a final l is [w]. Stress on the last syllable is the default for -l, so no accent.
Four forms: vermelho, vermelha, vermelhos, vermelhas. Spelling: lh is one sound [ʎ], like 'lli' in million: ver-MAY-lyoo.
One form for masculine and feminine. Plural verdes. The d comes before the weak final e, which is said i, so it is [dʒ]: VER-jee.

Also the noun a rosa, the flower. As a color it is left unchanged in everyday speech, because a bolsa rosa is a purse of the color of the rose. Said HAW-zuh: the initial r is the strong sound and s between vowels is [z].
Also the noun a cinza, ash. One form for masculine and feminine; the plural is cinza or cinzas. Spelling: c before i is [s], in is a nasal vowel, and the z starts a syllable so it is [z]: SEEN-zuh.

No separate feminine; plural marrons (a final m becomes ns). Spelling: rr is the strong r, and om at the end of a word is a nasal vowel, so the lips do not close: mah-HOHN. Stress on the last syllable, and -om is not a default for the second to last, so no accent.

example.pt: Os tênis marrons custam cento e cinquenta reais.
example.en: The brown sneakers cost one hundred fifty reais.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: d before i is [dʒ], nh is [ɲ], ei is a diphthong: jee-NYAY-roo. With a payment method, no article is used: em dinheiro.
The ending ão is a nasal diphthong, said like 'ow' in 'now' through the nose, and it is stressed: car-TÃO. The tilde marks the nasal sound and the stress together. Plural cartões.
The name of Brazil's instant payment system, written with a capital. Said PEEKS: one syllable, and x at the end is [ks], as in táxi.

From parcela, one portion of a total, and parcelar, to split into portions. It is an adjective made from the verb (stem parcel- plus -ado) and changes like any adjective in -o: parcelada, parcelados. Spelling: c before e is [s].

example.en: I want to pay in installments.

vocabulary.note: A vista is 'the sight': payable on sight, that is, in full at the moment of purchase rather than spread over months. It often earns a discount. The grave accent is the crase: the preposition a fused with the article a before the feminine noun vista.

example.pt: Eu pago à vista e tenho desconto.
example.en: I pay in one payment and get a discount.
example.literal: I-pay at-the sight and I-have discount.

vocabulary.note: Spelling: the s of des- closes a syllable ([s] or [ʃ] by region), c before o is [k], and on before t is a nasal vowel. The unstressed e of des- is often said i, so the d is [dʒ]: jees-KOHN-too.
Four forms: caro, cara, caros, caras. Que before an adjective makes an exclamation: Que caro! literally 'What expensive!', English 'How expensive!'.
Four forms: barato, barata, baratos, baratas.

The Brazilian currency. The plural is reais: a final l becomes is, like azul, azuis and qual, quais. Stress is on the last syllable in both (re-AL, re-AIS), the default for -l and -is. One hundredth of a real is um centavo.

A regular -ar verb whose subject is the thing that costs, so shopping talk needs mostly two forms: custa for one thing and custam for several. The s before t closes a syllable, so it is [s] or [ʃ] by region.

example.en: How much does this purse cost?

vocabulary.note: Means to try or test anything, and with clothes to try them on. Spelling: x before a consonant is [s], and the initial e is often said i: es-pe-ri-men-TAR; en is a nasal vowel.

example.en: I want to try on this coat.

vocabulary.note: To carry something along with you. In a shop Eu levo means 'I'll take it': you buy it and leave with it. The present tense states the decision.
Spelling: c before e is [s] and ei is a diphthong: ah-say-TAR. The thing accepted needs no article: aceitamos cartão.
One verb for both using and wearing: with clothes and sizes it means to wear. Spelling: s between vowels is [z]: oo-ZAR.
Regular -ar verb. It already contains the idea of 'for', so no extra word follows it: procuro uma bolsa, 'I look-for a purse'. Spelling: c before u is [k]: pro-ku-RAR.

example.en: I am looking for a black purse.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: reading the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every word in this unit can be read aloud with rules you already have. The method is the one from the first lessons. Split the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable, compare it with the default for the word's ending (an accent is written only when the word breaks the default), and then read each letter by its position. This note applies the method to the words that look hardest, so that no mark and no letter in the unit is a surprise. The table at the end lists each word with the rules that apply.

Start with the accents, because a written accent always has a reason. Tênis has two syllables, TÊ-nis, stressed on the first. The ending -is defaults to stress on the last syllable (as in reais), so stress on the first breaks the default and an accent is required. It is a circumflex because the stressed e is closed: a stressed e before an m or n that begins the next syllable is usually closed, the clue from the vowels lesson. Tênis is the same in the singular and the plural because a noun that ends in an unstressed -s does not change (o lápis, os lápis). Número has three syllables, NÚ-me-ro, stressed on the third to last, which no ending predicts, so it is always marked; u has only one quality, so the mark is the acute. Médio ('medium'), the word behind the size M, is MÉ-di-o for the same reason, with an open e. Dólar ('dollar'), the word you need for exchange rates, is DÓ-lar: the ending -r defaults to the last syllable, the stress is on the first, so it takes an accent, an acute because the o is open. Aí, 'there, near you', is a-Í: a stressed i alone in its syllable after another vowel is written í, which also stops it being read as the diphthong ai. Provador, cartão, azul and real are stressed on the last syllable, the default for endings in -r, -ão and -l, so none needs an accent.

The grave accent in à vista is the crase from the accents lesson. The preposition a met the article a before the feminine noun vista, and the two fused into one long a. The mark records that fusion; it does not mark stress and does not open the vowel.

Now the letters. A single s between two vowels is [z]: camiseta is ca-mi-ZE-ta, casaco is ca-ZA-co, rosa is RO-za and usar is u-ZAR. This is why ss exists, to write [s] between vowels (isso, esse). The cedilla makes c an [s] before a, o or u (calça, preço 'price'), and plain c is [s] before e or i (cinza, aceitar, cento). An l that closes a syllable is [w], not an English l: calça is KOW-suh, bolsa has the same w, and so do azul, qual, real and mil at the end of a word. The pairs nh and lh are single sounds and are never split in syllables: ta-ma-nho, di-nhei-ro, ver-me-lho, mi-lhão. Before the sound [i], which means an i or a weak final e, d is said [dʒ] and t is said [tʃ] in most Brazilian accents: verde is VER-jee, dinheiro starts with jee, vestido is ves-CHEE-do and este is ES-chee. The unstressed e of desconto is often said i, so its d is [dʒ] as well. After q, the u is silent before e or i (aquele, aquilo, quinhentos) and sounded [kw] before a (quanto, qual, quais, quarenta). A few words break this and sound the u before e or i, as the spelling reform note said; cinquenta, 'fifty', is one: seen-KWEN-ta, so cento e cinquenta has [kw] in it. The x of experimentar stands before a consonant, so it is [s]; the final x of Pix is [ks], as in táxi.

A nasal vowel is written with a vowel plus an n or m that closes the syllable, as in branco, cinza, cento, quanto, desconto and marrom, or with a tilde, as in cartão and milhão. The n or m is not pronounced as a consonant: the vowel itself is nasal. At the end of a word, em is [ẽj̃], said like 'ayn' through the nose, so cem sounds like SAYN. The strong r is written r at the start of a word (rosa, real) and rr between vowels (marrom); a single r between vowels is a tap (número, barato).

Finally, the clothing sizes P, M, G and GG are said with letter names from the alphabet lesson: pê, eme, gê and gê-gê.

grammar.title: Demonstratives: este, esse, aquele
grammar.explanation:
A demonstrative is a word that points at something and says where it is: English this, that, these and those. It does two jobs. Before a noun it stands where an article would stand (essa calça, 'this pair of pants') and it agrees with the noun in gender and number, as adjectives do. On its own it is a pronoun, a word that stands in for a noun (essa, 'this one'), which is possible whenever the listener already knows which noun is meant. English has two degrees of distance, this and that. Portuguese has three, and they are tied to the three grammatical persons from the grammar map: este points at what is near the speaker (first person), esse at what is near the listener (second person), and aquele at what is far from both (third person). The words for place follow the same three steps: aqui is here, near me; aí is there, near you; ali is over there, far from both.

The forms are built like the adjectives in -o, with -e or -a in the singular and -s in the plural: este, esta, estes, estas; esse, essa, esses, essas; aquele, aquela, aqueles, aquelas. The masculine singular ends in -e, not -o, and the spelling still follows the rules you know. The final e is weak and said i, so este is ES-chee, because t before the sound i is [tʃ] (as in tia and noite), while esse is ES-see with ss between vowels. Aquele has a silent u after q (ah-KAY-lee), and its stress falls on the second to last syllable, the default for a word that ends in e, so it needs no accent. This also explains the pair from the accents lesson: esta, 'this' (feminine), has no accent, while está, 'is', has one.

In everyday Brazilian speech the first step is weak. People say essa calça about a pair of pants in their own hands, and este and esta are mostly heard in writing and in careful or formal speech. Esse and essa therefore cover both 'near me' and 'near you', and the contrast that remains in speech is esse against aquele, near against far. To be exact, add aqui, aí or ali after the noun: essa calça aqui, aquele casaco ali. In a shop you will often hear esse aqui and aquele ali, said while pointing. When the noun is understood, English needs the stand-in word 'one'; Portuguese needs nothing, because the gender of the demonstrative already shows which noun is meant: essa custa cento e vinte reais.

Isto, isso and aquilo are the neutral demonstratives. Neuter means neither masculine nor feminine. Latin had a third gender, the neuter, and Portuguese nouns merged it into the masculine, but these three pronouns still show it. They name something whose gender you cannot know because you have not named it, or a whole situation or idea: O que é isso? 'What is that?' Because they stand for an unnamed thing, they never take a noun, never change form and never agree with anything. The -o of isso is the neutral ending, not the masculine one. With a noun you must use esse: esse casaco, never isso casaco.

Demonstratives fuse with the prepositions de and em, the same contractions you know from the articles: de + esse = desse, em + essa = nessa, de + aquele = daquele, em + aquela = naquela, de + isso = disso, em + isso = nisso. Because gostar is always followed by de, you say Eu gosto dessa bolsa and Eu gosto disso. The preposition a fuses with aquele and aquela into àquele and àquela, with the crase accent. Com and para do not fuse: com esse, para essa.

rows: near the speaker, in the textbook system
near the listener, and near the speaker too in everyday speech

grammar.title: Numbers from 100 to 1.000.000, and prices
grammar.explanation:
Portuguese builds a large number the way it built 21 to 99 (vinte e um): it says the parts from the largest to the smallest and joins the last steps with e, 'and'. The new part here is the hundred. The hundreds are words of their own, made from the unit plus -centos, 'hundreds', which is a plural: dois plus centos gives duzentos, 'two hundreds'. Three of them are irregular in spelling because they keep older forms of the unit, and must be learned as they stand: duzentos, trezentos and quinhentos. The others are regular: quatrocentos, seiscentos, setecentos, oitocentos, novecentos.

One hundred has two forms. Cem is the complete hundred, with nothing after it: cem reais, cem pessoas, and 1.100 is mil e cem. Cento is the form used when more follows: 101 is cento e um, 120 is cento e vinte. Both come from Latin centum; cem is the shortened form that appears when the hundred ends the number. The word centavo, one hundredth of a real, is cento plus -avo, the ending that makes 'the nth part' words, as in oitavo, an eighth. Between hundreds and tens, and between tens and units, e goes in: duzentos e trinta e cinco. Mil never changes (dois mil, dez mil), and no e follows it unless what comes next is below 100 or is a whole hundred: mil e quinhentos, mil e vinte, but mil duzentos e trinta.

Because the hundreds from 200 up are plural words, they agree with the noun they count, like an adjective: duzentos reais, because reais is masculine, but duzentas camisetas, because camiseta is feminine. Cem, cento and mil never change. The numbers one and two change in the way the numbers lesson showed (um and uma, dois and duas).

A million is not a number word like mil but a masculine noun: um milhão, with the plural milhões (ão becomes ões, as in the plurals lesson). Like any noun, it is joined to what is counted with de, as English does with 'a crowd of people': um milhão de reais, dois milhões de reais. Mil is not a noun, so mil reais has no de.

The currency is o real, plural reais (l becomes is, like azul and azuis). One hundredth of a real is um centavo. Prices are written with R$ before the number, but the word reais is said after it: R$ 30 is trinta reais. Write the decimals after a comma and group thousands with a period: R$ 1.250,50 is mil duzentos e cinquenta reais e cinquenta centavos. In a shop people shorten the price: R$ 49,90 is quarenta e nove e noventa. A percentage is por cento, literally 'by hundred': dez por cento is ten percent.

grammar.title: Colors: adjective agreement and the missing noun
grammar.explanation:
A color word is an adjective, a word that describes a noun, so every adjective rule from the grammar map applies. Portuguese puts the adjective after the noun: uma saia preta, literally 'a skirt black'. The logic is that the noun comes first and the adjective then narrows it down: a skirt, and which one? The black one. English does the opposite and puts the adjective first. Words that count or point (dois, essa, minha) come before the noun; descriptive words such as colors come after it.

The adjective copies the gender and number of its noun wherever it stands: a saia preta, as saias pretas, A saia é preta. Colors fall into three groups. First, colors ending in -o have four forms: branco, branca, brancos, brancas; preto, vermelho and amarelo ('yellow') work the same way. Second, colors ending in -e or in a consonant have no separate feminine and form the plural by the usual rules: verde, verdes; azul, azuis (l becomes is); marrom, marrons (m becomes ns). Third, some colors began as the name of a thing: rosa is the rose, laranja is the orange and cinza is ash. A bolsa rosa is a purse of the color of the rose, so the word is a noun in disguise and stays as it is whatever the gender or number of the thing described: duas bolsas rosa, camisetas laranja. This is the usual everyday form. You may also see rosas in writing, and cinza has the plural cinzas as well as cinza.

Words that say how much an adjective applies, such as muito (very) and um pouco (a little), are adverbs, and adverbs do not agree: uma bolsa muito cara, duas bolsas muito caras. Compare muito before a noun, which is an adjective and does agree: muitas bolsas. In Está um pouco cara, the adjective cara still agrees with the thing talked about, here a feminine purse, even though the word bolsa is not in the sentence.

Portuguese happily leaves out a noun the listener already knows. The article, number or demonstrative that stood before it keeps the gender and number, and English needs the stand-in word 'one'. Camila says Eu quero experimentar a azul. The a is the feminine article, so the missing noun is feminine (the calça), and azul is only the color. Carlos says uma vermelha e uma marrom, meaning two purses: the feminine uma and vermelha show it, and marrom has no feminine. The agreement is what tells you what is missing: a azul is the blue one if the noun is feminine, o azul if it is masculine. Demonstratives work the same way (essa, aquela).

To say light or dark, add claro or escuro with a hyphen: azul-claro, azul-escuro, verde-escuro. Traditional grammar makes only the last word agree (camisas azul-escuras), and everyday usage often leaves the whole expression unchanged (camisas azul-escuro); both are accepted, and a masculine singular noun avoids the question: um vestido azul-escuro.

grammar.title: Questions: quanto, qual and quais
grammar.explanation:
A question word stands where the missing information would be, and the rest of the sentence is an ordinary statement. As the grammar map showed, Portuguese puts the question word first and has no helper verb like English 'do': Quanto custa essa calça? is literally 'How-much costs this pant?' The subject can follow the verb, and Brazilians often move the question word to the end instead: Essa calça custa quanto?

Quanto means 'how much'. On its own, asking about a price, it does not change. Before a noun it behaves like an adjective and agrees: quantos reais, quantas camisetas. The verb agrees with the thing whose price you ask: custa for one thing, custam for several. The short forms use ser, 'to be': quanto é? for one thing or a total, quanto são? for several. Estar gives a third question, quanto está?, used when the price is a state that changes from moment to moment, such as an exchange rate: Quanto está o dólar hoje? This is the same contrast as in the ser and estar unit: ser for the standard fact, estar for how things are now. It also shows in the adjective. Essa bolsa é cara says the purse is an expensive thing. Está um pouco cara says its price strikes you as high at this moment, which is why bargaining uses estar.

Qual means 'which' and picks one from a set, such as sizes or colors: Qual é o seu tamanho? is literally 'Which is the your size?' The article before seu is normal in Brazil. English 'what' covers two jobs that Portuguese splits: o que asks what an unknown thing is (O que é isso?), and qual asks which one among a known set. Qual has no feminine form: qual calça, qual casaco. Its plural quais follows the rule for words that end in -al (animal, animais): Quais são as suas cores favoritas? Before a noun, qual and que are both heard: qual tamanho or que tamanho.

To ask for something, use eu queria, the polite form from the food unit, literally 'I wanted': Eu queria uma calça preta. To ask whether something exists, use tem, which is literally 'has' and also means 'there is' in everyday Brazilian speech: Tem desconto hoje?

grammar.title: Paying and bargaining: prepositions and fixed phrases
grammar.explanation:
Payment talk is made of short fixed phrases whose words are ordinary but whose combination is not always what English does. The governing idea is that Portuguese chooses the preposition by the role the noun plays in the action. Com, 'with', names the instrument: Eu pago com cartão, 'I-pay with card'. Em, 'in' or 'on', names the form or the setting of the payment: Eu pago em dinheiro, literally 'in money', and em três vezes, literally 'in three times', where vez is 'time' in the sense of 'occasion' and the plural is vezes, spelled with -es because the singular ends in z. In speech em fuses with the article, so pagar no cartão and pagar no Pix, literally 'in-the card' and 'in-the Pix', are as common as pagar com cartão and pagar com Pix; either is correct.

À vista and parcelado name the two basic ways to pay. À vista is literally 'at the sight': what is paid in plain sight, at the moment, in one payment. Parcelado is an adjective made from the verb parcelar, 'to split into portions'; a parcela is one portion, an installment. It agrees like any adjective in -o. Em três vezes says how many portions. Sem, 'without', gives sem desconto, 'without discount', and shops often give a discount for payment à vista or by Pix.

Bargaining uses everyday verbs in the plain present tense. Faz por oitenta? is literally 'Makes for eighty?' Fazer is 'to make' or 'to do', the subject 'you' is left out because the verb ending shows it, and por introduces the price 'for' which something is done: por oitenta. The seller answers Faço por noventa, 'I-make for ninety', meaning 'I'll let it go for ninety'. Fechado literally means 'closed': a deal that is closed is agreed. Eu levo literally says 'I carry', and in a shop it means 'I'll take it'; where English uses 'will' for a decision made on the spot, Portuguese uses the plain present. Aceitar takes no article before a payment method, because you are naming the kind of thing, not one particular item: Aceitamos cartão, 'We-accept card'.

culture.title: Pix, installments and bargaining
culture.text:
Brazil's instant payment system, Pix, is used everywhere: in shops, at street stalls and between friends. You pay by scanning a QR code or typing a key such as a phone number, and the money moves in seconds at no cost for people. Many small businesses prefer Pix to cash, so it is worth asking vocês aceitam Pix? before you pay.

Another common feature is parcelamento, paying in installments. Shops often let you pay in three, six or ten monthly installments, frequently with no interest (sem juros, literally 'without interest'), and prices are displayed as, for example, em dez vezes de vinte reais, literally 'in ten times of twenty reais'. Paying à vista, 'at sight', often earns a discount, and asking tem desconto? is normal in most shops. At a feira, a craft market, bargaining is accepted, and a polite faz mais barato? ('makes cheaper?') or um descontinho? is part of the game. The ending -inho means small and also softens a request: um descontinho is 'a little discount', which sounds friendlier than um desconto.

Forms of address matter at a market. Dona before a first name, as in Dona Rita, is a respectful title for an older woman, and its counterpart for a man is seu, as in seu João. Clothes come in P, M, G and GG, which stand for pequeno, médio, grande and extra grande. Shoes use numbers in the Brazilian system, usually from 34 to 44, so check the number rather than guess from another country's sizes. Prices are shown with R$ and a decimal comma.

exercises.prompt: Match each Portuguese phrase with its literal, word-for-word meaning
Why does tênis carry a written accent?
choices: The vowel is nasal, as a tilde would show
The stress is on the first syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in -is
It is borrowed from English, and borrowed words take an accent
It tells the word apart from têm
exercises.explanation: Words ending in -is are stressed on the last syllable by default. Tê-nis is stressed on the first, so an accent is required, and it is a circumflex because the stressed e is closed.

exercises.prompt: How is the l pronounced in calça (CAL-ça)?
choices: Like the l of English 'light'
It is silent
Like r
Like w, as at the end of English 'now'
exercises.explanation: An l that closes a syllable is [w]. The cedilla only makes the c an [s] before a.

exercises.prompt: Why is número written with an accent?
choices: It is stressed on the third to last syllable, and such words are always marked
Every word ending in o takes an accent
The u is a nasal vowel
It is a one-syllable word
exercises.explanation: Nú-me-ro has the stress on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts. The u has one quality, so the mark is the acute.

exercises.prompt: How is the single s of camiseta (ca-mi-SE-ta) pronounced?
choices: Like the s of English sun
Like z, because a single s between two vowels is voiced
Like sh
It is silent
exercises.explanation: A single s between two vowels is [z]. To write [s] between vowels the language doubles it: esse, isso.

exercises.prompt: In aquele, what does the u after q do?
choices: It is said as w, as in quanto
It makes the e nasal
It moves the stress onto that syllable
Nothing: it is silent, because qu before e or i is normally the sound [k]
exercises.explanation: Before e or i the u of qu is normally silent (aquele, aquilo, quinhentos). Before a it is sounded [kw] (quanto, qual). A few words such as cinquenta are exceptions.

exercises.audio_pt: Essa calça custa cento e vinte reais.
choices: These pants cost 220 reais.

exercises.prompt: Why does cartão carry a tilde and no other accent?
choices: The tilde marks an open vowel
The tilde replaces a missing n in the plural
The tilde marks the nasal sound and, with no other accent present, also the stress on the last syllable
The tilde shows the word is borrowed
exercises.explanation: The tilde makes the vowel nasal and, unless an acute or circumflex is present, also marks the stressed syllable: car-TÃO.

exercises.prompt: In the three-way system of demonstratives, which word points at something near the person you are speaking to?
choices: este
aquele
esse
isto
exercises.explanation: The three words follow the three persons: este for near the speaker, esse for near the listener, aquele for far from both.

exercises.hint_en: This blue T-shirt costs thirty reais.
exercises.explanation: Camiseta is feminine singular, so the demonstrative ends in -a. Essa is more usual in everyday speech.

exercises.explanation: Ali is the place word for far from both, and its demonstrative is aquele. Casaco is masculine.

exercises.prompt: You point at something you cannot name and ask what it is. Which question is correct?
choices: O que é essa?
O que é esse?
O que é isso?
O que é essas?
exercises.explanation: Isso is the neutral demonstrative. It names something whose gender you cannot know, never takes a noun and never changes.

choices: They are the same word spelled two ways
Está is plural
Está is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in a, so it needs the acute; esta is stressed on the first and needs nothing
Esta is the formal form
exercises.explanation: Words ending in a default to the second to last syllable. Está is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks that default, so the accent is required; es-ta is stressed on the first and follows it.

exercises.prompt: In 'Eu quero experimentar a azul', what is left out after azul?
choices: A masculine noun, such as casaco
The word um, which Portuguese needs where English says 'one'
Nothing: a azul is a fixed phrase
A feminine singular noun that is already known, such as calça
exercises.explanation: The a is the feminine singular article, so the understood noun is feminine singular. Azul is only the color.
Azul has no feminine form, and its plural follows the rule for words ending in -l: l becomes is.
Marrom has no feminine form, and a final m becomes ns in the plural.

exercises.prompt: Why is marrom written with no accent although it is stressed on the last syllable (mar-ROM)?
choices: A nasal vowel can never take an accent
The rr already marks the stress
It is a color word
The ending om is not among the endings that default to the second to last syllable, so the last syllable is the default and nothing breaks it
exercises.explanation: Only the endings a, e, o (with or without s), am, em and ens default to the second to last syllable. Any other ending defaults to the last, so mar-ROM is regular.

exercises.prompt: Carlos says 'Está um pouco cara' about a purse that he does not name in that sentence. Why is it cara and not caro?
choices: Um pouco makes an adjective feminine
Cara is the neutral form used after está
Cara agrees with the feminine noun bolsa, which is understood
Cara is the polite form
exercises.explanation: An adjective agrees with the noun it describes, even when the noun is understood from the previous sentence. Bolsa is feminine.

exercises.prompt: Why do we say 'duzentos reais' but 'duzentas camisetas'?

Duzentas is for plural nouns and duzentos for singular ones
Both forms are correct with either noun
exercises.explanation: Duzentos is a plural word made from 'hundreds', so it agrees with the counted noun like an adjective.
